title: Near Optimal Robust Federated Learning Against Data Poisoning Attack
claim: Poisoned workers can hide among honest ones, and whether their gradients stand out depends on model depth, which makes detection hard.
layout: 3 panels: system diagram left, two scatter plots right, shared legend
description: Panel (a) is a federated learning schematic. A dashed 'Server' box sits at the top and is linked by a bold bracket with arrows to a row of dashed worker boxes (Worker 1, Worker 2, Worker 3, ..., Worker m). Each worker holds a database cylinder. Workers 1 and 2 are red and labeled 'Poisoned data'. Workers 3 and m are blue and labeled 'Unpoisoned data'. A dashed 'Adversary' box at the bottom has thick arrows pointing up at the two red cylinders. Panels (b) and (c) are scatter plots of gradients projected onto two principal axes, with blue dots for normal gradients and a single red dot for the poisoned one. In (b) the red dot lies far from the blue cluster. In (c) the red dot sits inside the cluster, so it cannot be told apart. The eye goes first to the red and blue cylinders, then to the red dot's position in each plot.
caption: (a) Data poisoning attack in a federated learning system. (b-c) Two principal axes of gradients calculated by the same datasets on different neural networks. (b) The gradients are computed from a dense neural network (DNN) with 2 hidden layers and 128 neurons each hidden layer. (c) The gradients are computed from a DNN with 32 hidden layers and 128 neurons each hidden layer.
abstract: We revisit data poisoning attacks in the federated learning system. There will be $m$ worker nodes (each has $n$ training data samples) cooperatively training one model for a machine-learning task, and a fraction (i.e., $\alpha$) of the workers may suffer from the data poisoning attack. We mainly focus on the challenging and practical case where $n$ is small and $m$ is large, such that each worker does not have enough statistical information to identify the poisoned data by itself, while in total they have enough data to learn the task if the poisoned data are detected. Therefore, we propose a mechanism for workers to cooperatively detect workers with poisoned data. In terms of attack loss, our mechanism achieves $\tilde{O}((\frac{1}{n})^{\frac{1}{2}}+(\frac{d}{mn})^{\frac{1}{2}})$ in IID setting and $\tilde{O}((\frac{1}{\gamma})^{\frac{1}{2}}+(\frac{1}{n})^{\frac{1}{2}}+(\frac{d}{mn})^{\frac{1}{2}})$ in non-IID setting, where $d$ is the VC-dimension of the learning model and $\gamma$ is a concentration parameter characterizing the non-IIDness. Alongside attack loss, our mechanism limits the adversary’s free-ride gain even when it cannot be directly quantified by the attack loss. We also propose the lower bound of the attack loss, and our proposed algorithm matches the lower bound when $m\rightarrow \infty$ both in IID setting and non-IID setting.
